relations.note: Sopdu combines with Horus as Horus-Sopdu, an eastern falcon and royal power.
Sopdet generates Horus-Sopdu in astral birth language and is later treated as Sopdu’s mother.
Sah functions as Sopdu’s father within the astral family of Sah, Sopdet, and Sopdu.
relations.source: Pyramid Text and later astral theology

relations.note: Sopdu joins the divine coalition that responds to Seth’s assault and restores Osiris.
relations.source: Pyramid Text corpus and temple theology

relations.note: Isis is paralleled with Sopdet, making Horus-Sopdu analogous to her son Horus.
Later theology places Sopdu among divine powers judging and restraining Seth after his attack on Osiris.
relations.source: Pyramid Text traditions and temple theology

relations.note: Geb and Sopdu participate in the divine framework validating the resurrected king and opposing Seth.
Thoth and Sopdu occur together as divine authorities or judges within the Osirian and Horus–Seth complex.
Re addresses or recognizes the transformed king as Sopdu within eastern celestial theology.
Atum and Sopdu occur together in royal ascent and cosmic-allocation spells without a separate encounter.
Hathor governs turquoise while Sopdu represents and protects the eastern region at Serabit el-Khadim.
Khensit is Sopdu’s local consort, although no developed marriage narrative survives.
Some disputed local traditions call Shesmetet Sopdu’s mother, separately from the astral genealogy involving Sopdet.
Sopdu is fused with Shu as Shu-Sopdu or Sopdu-Shu, combining air, frontier force, and royal protection.
Tefnut and Sopdu belong to the coordinated divine group represented by the Nectanebid naoi.
Similar double-feathered and ithyphallic imagery encouraged context-dependent assimilation between Sopdu and Min.
Winged, knife-bearing Sopdu figures contributed to the development of composite Bes or Pantheos imagery.
Ptah and Sopdu share Serabit’s mining theology; occasional equations with a local Ptah form remain contested.
